lessons.title: Fundamentals of Time and Work
lessons.description: Understand work rates, efficiency and the relationship between work and time.
lessons.content:
Time and Work is an important quantitative aptitude topic used in placement examinations.

The fundamental relationship is:
Work = Rate × Time.

If a person completes a job in N days, the person's work rate is 1/N of the job per day.

Example 1: A completes a job in 10 days.
A's one-day work = 1/10.
Work completed in 3 days = 3/10.
Remaining work = 7/10.

Example 2: B completes a job in 15 days.
B's one-day work = 1/15.

When A and B work together, their rates are added:
Combined rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6.
Therefore, they complete the job together in 6 days.

Important formulas:
1. Work = Efficiency × Time.
2. Time = Total Work / Work Rate.
3. If A completes a job in a days and B in b days, their combined time is ab/(a+b), assuming constant independent work rates.
4. If efficiency increases, the time required for a fixed job decreases.

Placement tip: Convert every person's completion time into a one-day work rate before combining workers.

lessons.title: Combined Work and Individual Efficiency
lessons.description: Solve problems involving multiple workers and different efficiency levels.
lessons.content:
When two or more people work together, their individual work rates combine.

Example: A completes a job in 12 days and B in 18 days.
A's daily work = 1/12.
B's daily work = 1/18.
Combined work = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36.
Time together = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

Efficiency is the amount of work completed per unit time.

For the same amount of work, efficiency is inversely proportional to completion time.

If A is twice as efficient as B, A requires half as much time as B.

Example: A is twice as efficient as B. Together they complete a job in 12 days.
Let B's daily rate be x.
A's daily rate = 2x.
Combined rate = 3x = 1/12.
Therefore x = 1/36.
B alone takes 36 days.
A alone takes 18 days.

Three workers:
If A, B and C take a, b and c days individually, combined rate = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c.

Example: A takes 6 days, B takes 12 days and C takes 12 days.
Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 1/3.
Together they complete the work in 3 days.

Placement tip: Express efficiency ratios as daily work rates to avoid confusing efficiency with completion time.

lessons.title: Work and Wages
lessons.description: Learn how payment is distributed according to work contribution.
lessons.content:
Work and wages problems involve dividing payment among workers based on their contribution.

When workers receive payment proportional to the amount of work completed:
Wage Ratio = Work Contribution Ratio.

Work Contribution = Efficiency × Time Worked.

Example: A and B work for the same number of days. A is twice as efficient as B.
Their work ratio is 2:1.
If total wages are ₹9,000, A receives ₹6,000 and B receives ₹3,000.

Example: A works for 6 days at 3 units per day, while B works for 9 days at 2 units per day.
A's contribution = 6 × 3 = 18 units.
B's contribution = 9 × 2 = 18 units.
Their contributions are equal.
If total wages are ₹8,000, each receives ₹4,000.

For three workers, calculate each person's work contribution and divide total wages in that ratio.

Example: A, B and C contribute 20, 30 and 50 units of work.
Their ratio is 2:3:5.
For total wages of ₹10,000:
A receives ₹2,000.
B receives ₹3,000.
C receives ₹5,000.

Important: Equal working hours do not imply equal wages if workers have different productivity and payment is based on contribution.

Placement tip: Calculate work contribution first, simplify the ratio and then distribute wages.

lessons.title: Pipes and Cisterns
lessons.description: Solve tank-filling and emptying problems using positive and negative work rates.
lessons.content:
Pipes and cisterns problems use the same principles as Time and Work.

An inlet fills a tank and contributes a positive rate. An outlet empties a tank and contributes a negative rate.

If a pipe fills a tank in a hours, its filling rate is 1/a tank per hour.
If another pipe empties the tank in b hours, its emptying rate is -1/b tank per hour.

Net rate = Total filling rates - Total emptying rates.

Example: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and Pipe B fills it in 12 hours.
Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4.
The tank fills in 4 hours.

Example: An inlet fills a tank in 8 hours, while an outlet empties it in 12 hours.
Net rate = 1/8 - 1/12 = 1/24.
The initially empty tank fills in 24 hours when both remain open.

Example: Two inlet pipes fill a tank in 10 and 15 hours, while an outlet empties it in 30 hours.
Net rate = 1/10 + 1/15 - 1/30 = 2/15.
Time to fill = 15/2 = 7.5 hours.

If the net rate is zero, the tank level remains unchanged while all pipes operate. If the net rate is negative, an initially empty tank cannot be filled under those conditions.

Placement tip: Use positive signs for filling and negative signs for emptying.

lessons.title: Advanced Time and Work Problems
lessons.description: Solve alternate-day work, partial completion and changing workforce problems.
lessons.content:
Advanced Time and Work questions combine work rates with schedules, worker changes and partial completion.

Alternate-day work:
Example: A completes a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A.
A's rate = 1/10.
B's rate = 1/15.
Work completed in two days = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6.
After 10 days, they complete 5/6 of the job.
Remaining work = 1/6.
On day 11, A completes 1/10, leaving 1/15.
B completes the remaining 1/15 on day 12.
Total time = 12 days.

Partial work:
If A completes a job in 20 days, A completes 5/20 = 1/4 of the job in 5 days.
Remaining work = 3/4.

Changing workforce:
Example: A completes a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works alone for 3 days, then B joins.
A completes 3/12 = 1/4.
Remaining work = 3/4.
Combined daily rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36.
Time for remaining work = (3/4)/(5/36) = 27/5 = 5.4 days.
Total time = 3 + 5.4 = 8.4 days.

Men-days concept:
For workers of equal efficiency, total work is proportional to number of workers multiplied by working days and daily working hours.

Example: If 6 workers complete a job in 10 days, 12 equally efficient workers complete it in 5 days under identical working-hour conditions.

Problem-solving steps:
1. Identify individual work rates.
2. Split the schedule into phases.
3. Calculate work completed in each phase.
4. Subtract completed work from the total.
5. Calculate the time required for the remaining work.

Placement tip: For alternating schedules, calculate work in one full repeating cycle before handling the remaining fraction.

quizzes.explanation: A completes 1/4 in 3 days. Remaining work = 3/4. Combined rate = 5/36. Remaining time = 5.4 days. Total = 8.4 days.

exercises.title: Individual and Combined Work
exercises.description: Calculate how long two workers take to complete a job together.
exercises.instructions: A completes a job in 15 days and B in 20 days. Calculate their individual one-day work rates and the time required to complete the job together.

exercises.title: Efficiency Ratio Problem
exercises.description: Find individual completion times using efficiency ratios.
exercises.instructions: A is three times as efficient as B. Together they complete a job in 8 days. Find how many days A and B would each take individually.

exercises.title: Work and Wages Distribution
exercises.description: Distribute wages based on the work contributed by each person.
exercises.instructions: A works for 8 days at an efficiency of 3 units per day. B works for 6 days at an efficiency of 4 units per day. If total wages are ₹12,000, calculate each worker's share.

exercises.title: Pipes and Cisterns Challenge
exercises.description: Find the net filling time when multiple pipes operate simultaneously.
exercises.instructions: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours, Pipe B fills it in 15 hours and Pipe C empties it in 30 hours. If all three pipes are opened together when the tank is empty, calculate the time required to fill it.

exercises.title: Changing Workforce Problem
exercises.description: Solve a multi-stage time and work problem.
exercises.instructions: A completes a job in 16 days and B in 24 days. A works alone for 4 days, then B joins. Calculate the additional time required to finish the remaining work and the total completion time.
